1-import TS.StlcProp

5-
6---  # MoreStlc: More on the Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
7-
8---  ## Simple Extensions to STLC
9-
10---  The simply typed lambda-calculus has a rich enough structure to make
11---  its theoretical properties interesting, but it is not much of a
12---  programming language!
13---
14---  In this chapter, we begin to close the gap with real-world languages by
15---  introducing a number of familiar features that have straightforward
16---  treatments at the level of typing.
17-
18---  ### Numbers
19-
20---  As we saw in the `StlcExtended` exercises at the end of the StlcProp
21---  chapter, adding types, constants, and primitive operations for natural
22---  numbers is easy - basically just a matter of combining the Types and
23---  Stlc chapters. Adding more realistic numeric types like machine
24---  integers and floats is also straightforward, though of course the
25---  specifications of the numeric primitives become more fiddly.
26-
27---  When writing a complex expression, it is useful to be able to give
28---  names to some of its subexpressions to avoid repetition and increase
29---  readability. Most languages provide one or more ways of doing this. In
30---  OCaml and Haskell, for example, we can write `let x = t₁ in t₂` to mean
31---  "reduce the expression `t₁` to a value and bind the name `x` to this
32---  value while reducing `t₂`."
33---
34---  Our `let`-binder follows OCaml in choosing a standard *call-by-value*
35---  evaluation order, where the `let`-bound term must be fully reduced
36---  before reduction of the `let`-body can begin. The typing rule `let`
37---  tells us that the type of a `let` can be calculated by calculating the
38---  type of the `let`-bound term, extending the context with a binding with
39---  this type, and in this enriched context calculating the type of the
40---  body (which is then the type of the whole `let` expression).
41---
42---  At this point in the book, it's probably easier simply to look at the
43---  rules defining this new feature than to wade through a lot of English
44---  text conveying the same information. Here they are:
45-
46---  Syntax:
47---
48---        t ::=                   Terms
49---            | ...                 (other terms same as before)
50---            | let x = t₁ in t₂    let-binding
51---
52---  Reduction:
53---
54---                                       t₁ ⟶ t₁'
55---                           -------------------------------------        (let₁)
56---                           let x = t₁ in t₂ ⟶ let x = t₁' in t₂
57---
58---                              ---------------------------------         (letValue)
59---                              let x = v₁ in t₂ ⟶ [x := v₁] t₂
60---
61---  Typing:
62---
63---                   Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁      x ↦ τ₁ ; Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ τ₂
64---                   -------------------------------------------      (let)
65---                           Γ ⊢ let x = t₁ in t₂ ⦂ τ₂
66-
67---  ### Pairs
68-
69---  Our functional programming examples in Lean have made frequent use of
70---  *pairs* of values. The type of such a pair is called a *product type*.
71---
72---  The formalization of pairs is almost too simple to be worth discussing.
73---  However, let's look briefly at the various parts of the definition to
74---  emphasize the common pattern.
75-
76---  In Lean, there are two ways of extracting the components of a pair:
77---  *pattern matching* and the projection operators `fst` and `snd`. Just
78---  for fun, let's do our pairs the latter way. For example, here's how
79---  we'd write a function that takes a pair of numbers and returns the pair
80---  of their sum and difference:
81---
82---             λx : Nat × Nat.
83---                let sum = fst x + snd x in
84---                let diff = fst x - snd x in
85---                (sum, diff)
86-
87---  Adding pairs to the simply typed lambda-calculus, then, involves adding
88---  two new forms of term - pairing, written `(t₁,t₂)`, and projection,
89---  written `fst t` for the first projection from `t` and `snd t` for the
90---  second projection - plus one new type constructor, `τ₁ × τ₂`, called
91---  the *product* of `τ₁` and `τ₂`.
92-
93---  Syntax:
94---
95---             t ::=                Terms
96---                 | ...
97---                 | (t₁, t₂)         pair
98---                 | fst t            first projection
99---                 | snd t            second projection
100---
101---             v ::=                Values
102---                 | ...
103---                 | (v₁, v₂)         pair value
104---
105---             τ ::=                Types
106---                 | ...
107---                 | τ₁ × τ₂          product type
108-
109---  For reduction, we need several new rules specifying how pairs and
110---  projection behave.
111-
112---                                    t₁ ⟶ t₁'
113---                               --------------------                        (pair₁)
114---                               (t₁,t₂) ⟶ (t₁',t₂)
115---
116---                                    t₂ ⟶ t₂'
117---                               --------------------                        (pair₂)
118---                               (v₁,t₂) ⟶ (v₁,t₂')
119---
120---                                     t ⟶ t'
121---                                 ------------------                        (fst₁)
122---                                 fst t ⟶ fst t'
123---
124---                                ------------------                       (fstPair)
125---                                 fst (v₁,v₂) ⟶ v₁
126---
127---                                     t ⟶ t'
128---                                 ------------------                      (snd₁)
129---                                 snd t ⟶ snd t'
130---
131---                                ------------------                       (sndPair)
132---                                snd (v₁,v₂) ⟶ v₂
133-
134---  Rules `fstPair` and `sndPair` say that, when a fully reduced pair meets
135---  a first or second projection, the result is the appropriate component.
136---  The congruence rules `fst₁` and `snd₁` allow reduction to proceed under
137---  projections, when the term being projected from has not yet been fully
138---  reduced. `pair₁` and `pair₂` reduce the parts of pairs: first the left
139---  part, and then - when a value appears on the left - the right part. The
140---  ordering arising from the use of the metavariables `v` and `t` in these
141---  rules enforces a left-to-right evaluation strategy for pairs. (Note the
142---  implicit convention that metavariables like `v` and `v₁` can only
143---  denote values.) We've also added a clause to the definition of values,
144---  above, specifying that `(v₁,v₂)` is a value. The fact that the
145---  components of a pair value must themselves be values ensures that a
146---  pair passed as an argument to a function will be fully reduced before
147---  the function body starts executing.
148-
149---  The typing rules for pairs and projections are straightforward.
150-
151---                           Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁     Γ t₂ ⦂ τ₂
152---                          ------------------------------              (pair)
153---                            Γ ⊢(t₁, t₂) ⦂ τ₁ × τ₂
154---
155---                                 Γ ⊢ t ⦂ τ₁ × τ₂
156---                              -----------------------                  (fst)
157---                                  Γ ⊢ fst t ⦂ τ₁
158---
159---                                  Γ ⊢ t ⦂ τ₁ × τ₂
160---                              -----------------------                   (snd)
161---                                   Γ ⊢ snd t ⦂ τ₂
162-
163---  `pair` says that `(t₁, t₂)` has type `τ₁ × τ₂` if `t₁` has type `τ₁`
164---  and `t₂` has type `τ₂`. Conversely, `fst` and `snd` tell us that, if
165---  `t` has a product type `τ₁ × τ₂` (i.e., if it will reduce to a pair),
166---  then the types of the projections from this pair are `τ₁` and `τ₂`.

168---  ### Unit
169-
170---  Another handy base type is the singleton type `Unit`.
171-
172---  It has a single element - the term constant `unit` (with a small `u`) -
173---  and a typing rule making `unit` an element of `Unit`. We also add
174---  `unit` to the set of possible values - indeed, `unit` is the *only*
175---  possible result of reducing an expression of type `Unit`.
176-
177---  Syntax:
178---
179---             t ::=                Terms
180---                 | ...               (other terms same as before)
181---                 | unit              unit
182---
183---             v ::=                Values
184---                 | ...
185---                 | unit              unit value
186---
187---             τ ::=                Types
188---                 | ...
189---                 | Unit              unit type
190---
191---  Typing:
192---
193---                               ----------------                       (unit)
194---                               Γ ⊢ unit ⦂ Unit
195-
196---  It may seem a little strange to bother defining a type that has just
197---  one element -- after all, wouldn't every computation living in such a
198---  type be trivial?
199---
200---  This is a fair question, and indeed in the STLC the `Unit` type is not
201---  especially critical (though we'll see two uses for it below). Where
202---  `Unit` really comes in handy is in richer languages with *side effects*
203---  -- e.g., assignment statements that mutate variables or pointers,
204---  exceptions and other sorts of nonlocal control structures, etc. In such
205---  languages, it is convenient to have a type for the (trivial) result of
206---  an expression that is evaluated only for its effect.
207-
208---   ----------------------------------------

219-
220---  ### Sums
221-
222---  Many programs need to deal with values that can take two distinct
223---  forms. For example, we might identify students in a university database
224---  using *either* their name *or* their id number. A search function might
225---  return *either* a matching value *or* an error code.
226---
227---  These are specific examples of a binary *sum type* (sometimes called a
228---  *disjoint union*), which describes a set of values drawn from one of
229---  two given types, e.g.:
230---
231---             Nat + Bool
232-
233---  We create elements of these types by *tagging* elements of the
234---  component types. For example, if `n` is a `Nat` then `inl n` is an
235---  element of `Nat + Bool`; similarly, if `b` is a `Bool` then `inr b` is
236---  a `Nat + Bool`. The names of the tags `inl` and `inr` arise from
237---  thinking of them as functions
238---
239---             inl ⦂ Nat  → Nat + Bool
240---             inr ⦂ Bool → Nat + Bool
241---
242---  that "inject" elements of `Nat` or `Bool` into the left and right
243---  components of the sum type `Nat + Bool`. (But note that we don't
244---  actually treat them as functions in the way we formalize them: `inl`
245---  and `inr` are keywords, and `inl t` and `inr t` are primitive syntactic
246---  forms, not function applications.)
247-
248---  In general, the elements of a type `τ₁ + τ₂` consist of the elements of
249---  `τ₁` tagged with the token `inl`, plus the elements of `τ₂` tagged with
250---  `inr`.
251---
252---  (As we've seen in Lean programming, one important use of sums is
253---  signaling errors:
254---
255---            div ⦂ Nat → Nat → (Nat + Unit)
256---            div =
257---              λx:Nat. λy:Nat,
258---                if iszero y then
259---                  inr unit
260---                else
261---                  inl ...
262-
263---  The type `Nat + Unit` above is in fact isomorphic to `Option Nat` in
264---  Lean - i.e., it's easy to write functions that translate back and
265---  forth.
266---
267---  To *use* elements of sum types, we introduce a `case` construct (a very
268---  simplified form of Lean's `match`) to destruct them. For example, the
269---  following procedure converts a `Nat + Bool` into a `Nat`:
270-
271---          getNat ⦂ Nat+Bool → Nat
272---          getNat =
273---            λx:Nat+Bool,
274---              case x of
275---                inl n => n
276---              | inr b => if b then 1 else 0
277---
278---  More formally...
279---
280---  Syntax:
281---
282---             t ::=                Terms
283---                 | ...               (other terms same as before)
284---                 | inl τ₂ t₁         tagging (left)
285---                 | inr τ₁ t₂         tagging (right)
286---                 | case t of         case analysis
287---                     inl x₁ => t₁
288---                   | inr x₂ => t₂
289---
290---             v ::=                Values
291---                 | ...
292---                 | inl τ₂ v₁         tagged value (left)
293---                 | inr τ₁ v₂         tagged value (right)
294---
295---             τ ::=                Types
296---                 | ...
297---                 | τ₁ + τ₂           sum type
298---
299---  Reduction:
300---
301---                                     t₁ ⟶ t₁'
302---                              ------------------------                       (inl)
303---                              inl τ₂ t₁ ⟶ inl τ₂ t₁'
304---
305---                                     t₂ ⟶ t₂'
306---                              ------------------------                       (inr)
307---                              inr τ₁ t₂ ⟶ inr τ₁ t₂'
308---
309---                                     t ⟶ t'
310---                     -------------------------------------------            (case)
311---                      case t of inl x₁ => t₁ | inr x₂ => t₂ ⟶
312---                     case t' of inl x₁ => t₁ | inr x₂ => t₂
313---
314---                  -----------------------------------------------        (caseInl)
315---                  case (inl τ₂ v₁) of inl x₁ => t₁ | inr x₂ => t₂
316---                                 ⟶  [x₁ := v₁]t₁
317---
318---                  -----------------------------------------------        (caseInr)
319---                  case (inr τ₁ v₂) of inl x₁ => t₁ | inr x₂ => t₂
320---                                 ⟶  [x₂ := v₂]t₂
321---
322---  Typing:
323---
324---                                  Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁
325---                         ----------------------------                      (inl)
326---                             Γ ⊢ inl τ₂ t₁ ⦂ τ₁ + τ₂
327---
328---
329---                                Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ τ₂
330---                         ---------------------------                       (inr)
331---                           Γ ⊢ inr τ₁ t₂ ⦂ τ₁ + τ₂
332---
333---
334---                              Γ ⊢ t ⦂ τ₁ + τ₂
335---                           x₁ ↦ τ₁; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₃
336---                           x₂ ↦ τ₂; Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ τ₃
337---               ----------------------------------------------------        (case)
338---                   Γ ⊢ case t of inl x₁ => t₁ | inr x₂ => t₂ ⦂ τ₃
339---
340---  We use the type annotations on `inl` and `inr` to make the typing
341---  relation deterministic (each term has at most one type), as we did for
342---  functions.
343-
344---  Without this extra information, the typing rule `inl`, for example,
345---  would have to say that, once we have shown that `t₁` is an element of
346---  type `τ₁`, we can derive that `inl t₁` is an element of `τ₁ + τ₂` for
347---  *any* type `τ₂`. For example, we could derive both
348---  `inl 5 : Nat + Nat`and `inl 5 : Nat + Bool` (and infinitely many other
349---  types). This peculiarity (technically, a failure of uniqueness of
350---  types) would mean t hat we cannot build a typechecking algorithm simply
351---  by "reading the rules from bottom to top" as we could for all the other
352---  features seen so far.
353---
354---  There are various ways to deal with this difficulty. One simple one --
355---  which we've adopted here -- forces the programmer to explicitly
356---  annotate the "other side" of a sum type when performing an injection.
357---  This is a bit heavy for programmers (so real languages adopt other
358---  solutions), but it is easy to understand and formalize.
359-

372---          (A)  (λx : Nat + Bool.

374---                    inl n => n + 3
375---                    | inr b => 0

380---          (C)  case inl Bool 4 of
381---                 inl n => n + 3

423-
424---  ### Lists
425-
426---  The typing features we have seen can be classified into *base types*
427---  like `Bool`, and *type constructors* like `→` and `×` that build new
428---  types from old ones. Another useful type constructor is `List`. For
429---  every type `τ`, the type `List τ` describes finite-length lists whose
430---  elements are drawn from `τ`.
431---
432---  In principle, we could encode lists using pairs, sums, unit, and
433---  *recursive* types. But giving semantics to recursive types is
434---  non-trivial. Instead, we'll just discuss the special case of lists
435---  directly.
436---
437---  Below we give the syntax, semantics, and typing rules for lists. Except
438---  for the fact that explicit type annotations are mandatory on `nil` and
439---  cannot appear on `cons`, these lists are essentially identical to those
440---  we built in Rocq. We use `case`, rather than `head` and `tail`
441---  operators, to destruct lists, to avoid dealing with questions like
442---  "what is the `head` of the ∅ list?"
443---
444---  For example, here is a function that calculates the sum of the first
445---  two elements of a list of numbers:
446---
447---  λ x:List Nat. case x of nil => 0 | a :: x' => case x' of nil => a | b
448---  :: x'' => a + b
449-
450---  Syntax:
451---
452---             t ::=                Terms
453---                 | ...
454---                 | nil τ             ∅ list
455---                 | t₁ :: t₂          cons
456---                 | case t₁ of        case analysis
457---                     nil      => t₂
458---                     | xh::xt => t₃
459---
460---             v ::=                Values
461---                 | ...
462---                 | nil τ             nil value
463---                 | v₁ :: v₂          cons value
464---
465---             τ ::=                Types
466---                 | ...
467---                 | List τ            list of τs
468---
469---  Reduction:
470---
471---                                      t₁ ⟶ t₁'
472---                             --------------------------                    (cons₁)
473---                               t₁ :: t₂ ⟶ t₁' :: t₂
474---
475---                                      t₂ ⟶ t₂'
476---                             --------------------------                    (cons₂)
477---                               v₁ :: t₂ ⟶ v₁ :: t₂'
478---
479---                                    t₁ ⟶ t₁'
480---                      -------------------------------------------         (listCase₁)
481---                       (case t₁ of nil => t₂ | xh :: xt => t₃) ⟶
482---                      (case t₁' of nil => t₂ | xh :: xt => t₃)
483---
484---                     ------------------------------------------          (listCaseNil)
485---                     (case nil τ₁ of nil => t₂ | xh :: xt => t₃)
486---                                      ⟶ t₂
487---
488---                    -------------------------------------------         (listCaseCons)
489---                    (case (vh :: vt) of nil => t₂ | xh :: xt => t₃)
490---                                ⟶ [xh:=vh][xt:=vt] t₃
491---
492---  Typing:
493---
494---                              ----------------------------                    (nil)
495---                              Γ ⊢ nil τ₁ ⦂ List τ₁
496---
497---                           Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁      Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ List τ₁
498---                  -------------------------------------------------           (cons)
499---                               Γ ⊢ t₁ :: t₂ ⦂ List τ₁
500---
501---                              Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ List τ₁
502---                              Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ τ₂
503---                        (xh ↦ τ₁; xt ↦ List τ₁; Γ) ⊢ t₃ ⦂ τ₂
504---                ----------------------------------------------------         (listCase)
505---                   Γ ⊢ (case t₁ of nil => t₂ | xh :: xt => t₃) ⦂ τ₂
506-
507---  ### General Recursion
508-
509---  Another facility found in most programming languages (including Lean)
510---  is the ability to define recursive functions. For example, we would
511---  like to be able to define and use the factorial function like this:
512---
513---            let fact = λx:Nat.
514---                         if x=0 then 1 else x * (fact (pred x))) in
515---            fact 3.
516---
517---  Note that the right-hand side of this binder mentions `fact`, the
518---  variable being bound - something that is not allowed according to the
519---  way we defined `let` above.
520-
521---  (The body of a `let` is typechecked in the same context as the `let`
522---  itself, which means that the recursive occurrence of `fact` in the body
523---  will not have a type in the context when it is looked up by the `var`
524---  rule.)
525-
526---  Changing the `let` rule to handle "recursive definitions" like this is
527---  possible, but it requires some extra effort -- e.g., passing around an
528---  extra "environment" of recursive function definitions in the definition
529---  of the `step` relation. We're going to take a simpler path here.
530-
531---  Here is another way of presenting recursive functions that is a bit
532---  more verbose but equally powerful and much more straightforward to
533---  formalize: instead of writing recursive definitions, we will define a
534---  *fixed-point operator* called `fix` that performs the "unfolding" of
535---  the recursive definition in the right-hand side as needed, during
536---  reduction.
537---
538---  For example, instead of
539---
540---            fact = λax:Nat.
541---                      if x=0 then 1 else x * (fact (pred x)))
542---
543---  we will write:
544-
545---  fact =
546---            fix
547---              (λaf:Nat → Nat.
548---                 λx:Nat.
549---                    if x=0 then 1 else x * (f (pred x)))
550-
551---  We can derive the latter from the former as follows:
552---
553---  - In the right-hand side of the definition of `fact`, replace recursive
554---    references to `fact` by a fresh variable `f`.
555---
556---  - Add an abstraction binding `f` at the front, with an appropriate type
557---    annotation. (Since we are using `f` in place of `fact`, which had
558---    type `Nat→Nat`, we should require `f` to have the same type.) The new
559---    abstraction has type `(Nat→Nat) → (Nat→Nat)`.
560---
561---  - Apply `fix` to this abstraction. This application has type `Nat→Nat`.
562---
563---  - Use all of this as the right-hand side of an ordinary `let`-binding
564---    for `fact`.
565-
566---  For the mathematically inclined, the intuition here is that the
567---  higher-order function `f` passed to `fix` is a *generator* for the
568---  `fact` function: if `f` is applied to a function that "approximates"
569---  the desired behavior of `fact` up to some number `n` (that is, a
570---  function that returns correct results on inputs less than or equal to
571---  `n` but we don't care what it does on inputs greater than `n`), then
572---  `f` returns a slightly better approximation to `fact` -- a function
573---  that returns correct results for inputs up to `n+1`. Applying `fix` to
574---  this generator returns its *fixed point*, which is a function that
575---  gives the desired behavior for all inputs `n`.
576---
577---  (The term "fixed point" is used here in exactly the same sense as in
578---  ordinary mathematics, where a fixed point of a function `f` is an input
579---  `x` such that `f(x) = x`. Here, a fixed point of a function `F` of type
580---  `(Nat→Nat)→(Nat→Nat)` is a function `f` of type `Nat→Nat` such that
581---  `F f` behaves the same as `f`.)
582-
583---  Syntax:
584---
585---             t ::=                Terms
586---                 | ...
587---                 | fix t₁            fixed-point operator
588---
589---  Reduction:
590---
591---                                      t₁ ⟶ t₁'
592---                                  ------------------                   (fix₁)
593---                                  fix t₁ ⟶ fix t₁'
594---
595---                     --------------------------------------------      (fixAbs)
596---                     fix (λxf:τ₁.t₁) ⟶ [xf:=fix (λxf:τ₁.t₁)] t₁
597---
598---  Typing:
599---
600---                                 Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁ → τ₁
601---                                 ------------------                    (fix)
602---                                 Γ ⊢ fix t₁ ⦂ τ₁
603-
604---  Let's see how `fixAbs` works by reducing `fact 3 = fix F 3`, where
605---
606---          F = (λf. λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (f (pred x)))
607---
608---  (type annotations are omitted for brevity).
609---
610---          fix F 3
611---
612---      ⟶ fixAbs + app₁
613---
614---          (λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) 3
615---
616---      ⟶ appAbs
617---
618---          if 3=0 then 1 else 3 * (fix F (pred 3))
619---
620---      ⟶ if0Nonzero
621---
622---          3 * (fix F (pred 3))
623---
624---      ⟶ fixAbs + mult₂ + app₁
625---
626---          3 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) (pred 3))
627---
628---      ⟶ predNat + mult₂ + app₂
629---
630---          3 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) 2)
631---
632---      ⟶ appAbs + mult₂
633---
634---          3 * (if 2=0 then 1 else 2 * (fix F (pred 2)))
635---
636---      ⟶ if0Nonzero + mult₂
637---
638---          3 * (2 * (fix F (pred 2)))
639---
640---      ⟶ fixAbs + 2 × mult₂ + app₁
641---
642---          3 * (2 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) (pred 2)))
643---
644---      ⟶ predNat + 2 x mult₂ + app₂
645---
646---          3 * (2 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) 1))
647---
648---      ⟶ appAbs + 2 x mult₂
649---
650---          3 * (2 * (if 1=0 then 1 else 1 * (fix F (pred 1))))
651---
652---      ⟶ if0Nonzero + 2 x mult₂
653---
654---          3 * (2 * (1 * (fix F (pred 1))))
655---
656---      ⟶ fixAbs + 3 x mult₂ + app₁
657---
658---          3 * (2 * (1 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) (pred 1))))
659---
660---      ⟶ predNat + 3 × mult₂ + app₂
661---
662---          3 * (2 * (1 * ((λx. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fix F (pred x))) 0)))
663---
664---      ⟶ appAbs + 3 × mult₂
665---
666---          3 * (2 * (1 * (if 0=0 then 1 else 0 * (fix F (pred 0)))))
667---
668---      ⟶ if0Zero + 3 x mult₂
669---
670---          3 * (2 * (1 * 1))
671---
672---      ⟶ multNats + 2 x mult₂
673---
674---          3 * (2 * 1)
675---
676---      ⟶ multNats + mult₂
677---
678---          3 * 2
679---
680---      ⟶ multNats
681---
682---          6
683---
684---  The simply typed lambda-calculus with fixed points is a famous and
685---  extensively studied system. It is often called *PCF* because it is a
686---  simple language of "partial computable functions".

738---  ### Exercise (1 star): fact_steps (Optional) ⭐
739-
740---  Write down the sequence of steps that the term `fact 1` goes through to
741---  reduce to a normal form (assuming the usual reduction rules for
742---  arithmetic operations.
743-
744---              fact 1
745---            = fix (λf:Nat→Nat. λx:Nat. if x=0 then 1 else x * (f (pred x))) 1
746---          ⟶ (λx: Nat, if x = 0 then 1 else x * (fact (pred x))) 1

750---          ⟶ 1 * ((λx:Nat. if x=0 then 1 else x * (fact (pred x))) 0)

756-
757---  The ability to form the fixed point of a function of type `τ→τ` for any
758---  `τ` has some surprising consequences. In particular, it implies that
759---  *every* type is inhabited by some term. To see this, observe that, for
760---  every type `τ`, we can define the term:
761---
762---          fix (λx:τ,x)
763---
764---  By `fix` and `abs`, this term has type `τ`. By `fixAbs` it reduces to
765---  itself, over and over again. Thus it is a *diverging element* of `τ`.
766---
767---  More usefully, here's an example using `fix` to define a two-argument
768---  recursive function:
769---
770---          equal =
771---            fix
772---              (\eq:Nat→Nat→Bool.
773---                 \m:Nat. \n:Nat.
774---                   if m=0 then iszero n
775---                   else if n=0 then false
776---                   else eq (pred m) (pred n))
777---
778---  And finally, here is an example where `fix` is used to define a *pair*
779---  of recursive functions (illustrating the fact that the type `τ₁` in the
780---  rule `fix` need not be a function type):
781---
782---          let evenodd =
783---               fix
784---                 (\eo: ((Nat → Nat) * (Nat → Nat)).
785---                    (\n:Nat. if0 n then 1 else (snd eo (pred n)),
786---                     \n:Nat. if0 n then 0 else (fst eo (pred n)))) in
787---          let even = fst evenodd in
788---          let odd  = snd evenodd in
789---          (even 3, even 4)}
790-
791---  ## Records
792-
793---  As a final example of a basic extension of the STLC, let's look briefly
794---  at how to define *records* and their types. Intuitively, records can be
795---  obtained from pairs by two straightforward generalizations: they are
796---  n-ary (rather than just binary) and their fields are accessed by
797---  *label* (rather than position).
798-
799---  Syntax:
800---
801---             t ::=                          Terms
802---                 | ...
803---                 | {i₁=t₁, ..., in=tn}        record
804---                 | t.i                        projection
805---
806---             v ::=                          Values
807---                 | ...
808---                 | {i₁=v₁, ..., in=vn}         record value
809---
810---             τ ::=                          Types
811---                 | ...
812---                 | {i₁:τ₁, ..., in:τn}         record type
813-
814---  The generalization from products should be pretty obvious. But it's
815---  worth noticing the ways in which what we've actually written is even
816---  *more* informal than the informal syntax we've used in previous
817---  sections and chapters: we've used "`...`" in several places to mean
818---  "any number of these," and we've omitted explicit mention of the usual
819---  side condition that the labels of a record should not contain any
820---  repetitions.
821-
822---  Reduction:
823---
824---                                    ti ⟶ ti'
825---                       ------------------------------------                  (rcd)
826---                           {i₁=v₁, ..., im=vm, in=ti , ...}
827---                       ⟶ {i₁=v₁, ..., im=vm, in=ti', ...}
828---
829---                                    t ⟶ t'
830---                                  --------------                           (proj₁)
831---                                  t.i ⟶ t'.i
832---
833---                            -------------------------                    (projRcd)
834---                            {..., i=vi, ...}.i ⟶ vi
835-
836---  Again, these rules are a bit informal. For example, the first rule is
837---  intended to be read "if `ti` is the leftmost field that is not a value
838---  and if `ti` steps to `ti'`, then the whole record steps..." In the last
839---  rule, the intention is that there should be only one field called `i`,
840---  and that all the other fields must contain values.
841-
842---  The typing rules are also simple:
843---
844---                     Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ τ₁     ...     Γ ⊢ tn ⦂ Tn
845---                -----------------------------------------------------        (rcd)
846---                Γ ⊢ {i₁=t₁, ..., in=tn} ⦂ {i₁:τ₁, ..., in:Tn}
847---
848---
849---                            Γ ⊢ t ⦂ {..., i:Ti, ...}
850---                          ---------------------------------                  (proj)
851---                                Γ ⊢ t.i ⦂ Ti
852-
853---  There are several ways to approach formalizing the above definitions.
854---
855---  - We can directly formalize the syntactic forms and inference rules,
856---    staying as close as possible to the form we've given them above. This
857---    is conceptually straightforward, and it's probably what we'd want to
858---    do if we were building a real compiler (in particular, it will allow
859---    us to print error messages in the form that programmers will find
860---    easy to understand). But the formal versions of the rules will not be
861---    very pretty or easy to work with, because all the `...`s above will
862---    have to be replaced with explicit quantifications or comprehensions.
863---    For this reason, records are not included in the extended exercise at
864---    the end of this chapter. (It is still useful to discuss them
865---    informally here because they will help motivate the addition of
866---    subtyping to the type system when we get to the Sub chapter.)
867---
868---  - Alternatively, we could look for a smoother way of presenting records
869---    -- for example, a binary presentation with one constructor for the ∅
870---    record and another constructor for adding a single field to an
871---    existing record, instead of a single monolithic constructor that
872---    builds a whole record at once. This is the right way to go if we are
873---    primarily interested in studying the metatheory of the calculi with
874---    records, since it leads to clean and elegant definitions and proofs.
875---
876---  - Finally, if we like, we can avoid formalizing records altogether, by
877---    stipulating that record notations are just informal shorthands for
878---    more complex expressions involving pairs and product types. We sketch
879---    this approach in the next section.
880-
881---  Let's see how records can be encoded using just pairs and `unit`. (This
882---  clever encoding, as well as the observation that it also extends to
883---  systems with subtyping, is due to Luca Cardelli.)
884---
885---  First, observe that we can encode arbitrary-size *tuples* using nested
886---  pairs and the `unit` value. To avoid overloading the pair notation
887---  `(t₁,t₂)`, we'll use curly braces without labels to write down tuples,
888---  so `{}` is the ∅ tuple, `{5}` is a singleton tuple, `{5,6}]`is a
889---  2-tuple (morally the same as a pair), `{5,6,7}` is a triple, etc.
890---
891---            {}                 ⟶  unit
892---            {t₁, t₂, ..., tn}  ⟶  (t₁, trest)
893---                                      where {t₂, ..., tn} ⟶ trest
894---
895---  Similarly, we can encode tuple types using nested product types:
896---
897---            {}                 ⟶  Unit
898---            {τ₁, τ₂, ..., Tn}  ⟶  τ₁ * TRest
899---                                      where {τ₂, ..., τn} ⟶ τn
900---
901---  The operation of projecting a field from a tuple can be encoded using a
902---  sequence of second projections followed by a first projection:
903---
904---            t.0        ⟶  fst t
905---            t.(n+1)    ⟶  (snd t).n
906---
907---  Next, suppose that there is some total ordering on record labels, so
908---  that we can associate each label with a unique natural number. This
909---  number is called the *position* of the label. For example, we might
910---  assign positions like this:
911---
912---            LABEL   POSITION
913---            a       0
914---            b       1
915---            c       2
916---            ...     ...
917---            bar     1395
918---            ...     ...
919---            foo     4460
920---            ...     ...
921---
922---  We use these positions to encode record values as tuples (i.e., as
923---  nested pairs) by sorting the fields according to their positions. For
924---  example:
925---
926---            {a=5,b=6}       ⟶   {5,6}
927---            {a=5,c=7}       ⟶   {5,unit,7}
928---            {c=7,a=5}       ⟶   {5,unit,7}
929---            {c=5,b=3}       ⟶   {unit,3,5}
930---            {f=8,c=5,a=7}   ⟶   {7,unit,5,unit,unit,8}
931---            {f=8,c=5}       ⟶   {unit,unit,5,unit,unit,8}
932---
933---  Note that each field appears in the position associated with its label,
934---  that the size of the tuple is determined by the label with the highest
935---  position, and that we fill in unused positions with `unit`.
936---
937---  We do exactly the same thing with record types:
938---
939---            {a:Nat,b:Nat}       ⟶   {Nat,Nat}
940---            {c:Nat,a:Nat}       ⟶   {Nat,Unit,Nat}
941---            {f:Nat,c:Nat}       ⟶   {Unit,Unit,Nat,Unit,Unit,Nat}
942---
943---  Finally, record projection is encoded as a tuple projection from the
944---  appropriate position:
945---
946---            t.l ⟶ t.(position of l)
947---
948---  It is not hard to check that all the typing rules for the original
949---  "direct" presentation of records are validated by this encoding. (The
950---  reduction rules are "almost validated" -- not quite, because the
951---  encoding reorders fields.)
952-
953---  Of course, this encoding will not be very efficient if we happen to use
954---  a record with label `foo`! But things are not actually as bad as they
955---  might seem: for example, if we assume that our compiler can see the
956---  whole program at the same time, we can *choose* the numbering of labels
957---  so that we assign small positions to the most frequently used labels.
958---  Indeed, there are industrial compilers that essentially do this!
959-
960---  Just as products can be generalized to records, sums can be generalized
961---  to n-ary labeled types called *variants*. Instead of `τ₁+τ₂`, we can
962---  write something like `<l₁:τ₁,l₂:τ₂,...ln:τn>` where `l₁`,`l₂`,... are
963---  field labels which are used both to build instances and as case arm
964---  labels.
965---
966---  These n-ary variants give us almost enough mechanism to build arbitrary
967---  inductive data types like lists and trees from scratch -- the only
968---  thing missing is a way to allow *recursion* in type definitions. We
969---  won't cover this here, but detailed treatments can be found in many
970---  textbooks -- e.g., Types and Programming Languages (Pierce, 2002).
971-
972---  ### Exercise: Formalizing the Extensions
973-
974---  In this series of exercises, you will formalize some of the extensions
975---  described in this chapter. We've provided the necessary additions to
976---  the syntax of terms and types, and we've included a few examples that
977---  you can test your definitions with to make sure they are working as
978---  expected. You'll fill in the rest of the definitions and extend all the
979---  proofs accordingly.
980---
981---  To get you started, we've provided implementations for:
982---
983---  - numbers
984---  - sums
985---  - lists
986---  - unit
987---
988---  You need to complete the implementations for:
989---
990---  - pairs
991---  - let (which involves binding)
992---  - fix
993---
994---  A good strategy is to work on the extensions one at a time (first
995---  pairs, then let, then fix), in separate passes, rather than trying to
996---  do all three at once in a single pass. For each definition or proof,
997---  begin by reading carefully through the parts that are provided for you,
998---  referring to the text in the Stlc chapter for high-level intuitions and
999---  the embedded comments for detailed mechanics.
1000-
1001---  Syntax:
1002-
1003-namespace StlcExtended
1004-

1040-

1105-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
1106-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)

1112-      | "fst" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`fst` must be applied to an argument"
1113-      | "snd" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`snd` must be applied to an argument"
1114-      | "nil" => Macro.throwErrorAt x  "`nil` must be applied to an argument"
1115-      | "pred" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`pred` must be applied to an argument"
1116-      | "inl" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`inl` must be applied to two arguments"

1118-      | "fix" => Macro.throwErrorAt x  "`fix` must be applied to an argument"

1128-          | "pred" => `(Tm.pred <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)

1163-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
1164-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
1165-  Stlc.isPlainName s && s != "Nat" && s != "succ" && s != "pred" && s != "unit"
1166-    && s != "Unit" && s != "inl" && s != "inr" && s != "if0" && s != "case" && s != "nil"
1167-    && s != "fix"

1169-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1170-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
1171-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
1172-  let stx ←
1173-    match_expr ← getExpr with
1174-    | Ty.nat => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
1175-    | Ty.unit => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Unit):ident)
1176-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
1177-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1178-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
1179-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
1180-    | Ty.prod _ _ => do
1181-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1182-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
1183-        `(stlcTy| $a × $b)
1184-    | Ty.sum _ _ => do
1185-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1186-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
1187-        `(stlcTy| $a + $b)
1188-    | Ty.list _ => do
1189-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
1190-        `(stlcTy| [$b] )
1191-    | _ => do
1192-        match ← delab with
1193-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
1194-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
1195-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
1196-
1197-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1198-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
1199-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
1200-  let stx ←
1201-    match_expr ← getExpr with
1202-    | Tm.var _ => do
1203-        let x ← withAppArg delab
1204-        match x with
1205-        | `($s:str) =>
1206-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
1207-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
1208-            else
1209-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``Tm.var
1210-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
1211-        | _ =>
1212-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``Tm.var
1213-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
1214-    | Tm.const _ => do
1215-        let n ← withAppArg delab
1216-        match n with
1217-        | `($n:num) => `(stlcTm| $n:num)
1218-        | _ =>
1219-            let const : Term := mkIdent ``Tm.const
1220-            `(stlcTm| ~($const $n))
1221-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
1222-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1223-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1224-        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
1225-    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
1226-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg Stlc.delabVarInner
1227-        let τ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1228-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1229-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $τ . $t)
1230-    | Tm.letIn _ _ _ => do
1231-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg Stlc.delabVarInner
1232-        let t₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1233-        let t₂ ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1234-        `(stlcTm| let $x = $t₁ in $t₂)
1235-    | Tm.succ _ => do
1236-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner

1309-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1310-@[delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.nat, delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.arrow, delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.unit,
1311-  delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.prod, delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.sum, delab app.StlcExtended.Ty.list]
1312-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1313-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
1314-    | Ty.nat => true | Ty.arrow _ _ => true
1315-    | Ty.prod _ _ => true | Ty.sum _ _ => true
1316-    | Ty.list _ => true | Ty.unit => true | _ => false
1317-  match ← delabTyInner with
1318-  | `(stlcTy| ~$e) => pure e
1319-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTy }>)

1321-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1322-@[delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.var, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.app, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.abs,
1323-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.const, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.succ, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.pred,
1324-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.mult, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.ite0, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.listNil,
1325-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.listCons, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.listCase,
1326-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.sumInl, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.sumInr,
1327-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.sumCase, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.pair,
1328-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.fst, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.snd, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.unit,
1329-  delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.letIn, delab app.StlcExtended.Tm.fix ]
1330-def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1331-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
1332-    | Tm.var _ => true | Tm.app _ _ => true | Tm.abs _ _ _ => true
1333-    | Tm.const _ => true | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true
1334-    | Tm.mult _ _ => true | Tm.ite0 _ _ _ => true
1335-    | Tm.unit => true | Tm.fix _ => true | Tm.letIn _ _ _ => true
1336-    | Tm.sumInl _ _ => true | Tm.sumInr _ _ => true | Tm.sumCase _ _ _ _ _ => true
1337-    | Tm.listNil _ => true | Tm.listCons _ _ => true | Tm.listCase _ _ _ _ _ => true
1338-    | Tm.pair _ _ => true | Tm.fst _ => true | Tm.snd _ => true
1339-    | _ => false
1340-  match ← delabTmInner with
1341-  | `(stlcTm| ~($e)) => pure e
1342-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
1343-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)

1354-def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
1355-  match t with
1356-  -- pure STLC
1357-  | .var y =>
1358-      if x = y then s else t
1359-  | <{ λ ~y : ~τ . ~t₁}> =>
1360-      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~τ . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
1361-  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
1362-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
1363-  -- numbers
1364-  | .const _ =>
1365-      t
1366-  | <{ succ ~t₁ }> =>
1367-      <{ succ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }>
1368-  | <{ pred ~t₁ }> =>
1369-      <{ pred ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }>
1370-  | <{ ~t₁ * ~t₂ }> =>
1371-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) * ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
1372-  | <{ if0 ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
1373-      <{ if0 [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
1374-  -- sums
1375-  | .sumInl τ₂ t₁ =>
1376-      <{inl ~τ₂ ( [~x:= ~s] ~t₁) }>
1377-  | .sumInr τ₂ t₁ =>
1378-      <{inr ~τ₂ ( [~x:= ~s] ~t₁) }>
1379-  | <{case ~t of inl ~x₁ => ~t₁ | inr ~x₂ => ~t₂}> =>
1380-      let t₁ := if x = x₁ then t₁ else <{ [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
1381-      let t₂ := if x = x₂ then t₂ else <{ [~x := ~s] ~t₂ }>
1382-      <{case ([~x := ~s] ~t) of inl ~x₁ => ~t₁ | inr ~x₂ => ~t₂ }>
1383-  -- lists
1384-  | .listNil _ => t
1385-  | <{~t₁ :: ~t₂}> =>
1386-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) :: [~x := ~s] ~t₂ }>

1390-          nil => [~x := ~s] ~t₂
1391-        | ~x₁ :: ~x₂ =>  ~t₃ }>

1393-  | .unit => <{ unit }>

1427---  Next we define the values of our language.

1429-inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
1430-  -- In pure STLC, function abstractions are values:
1431-  | abs (x : String) (τ₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : IsValue <{λ ~x : ~τ₂ . ~t₁}>
1432-  -- Numbers are values:
1433-  | nat (n : Nat) : IsValue (.const n)
1434-  -- A tagged value is a value:
1435-  | sumInl (v : Tm) (τ₁ : Ty) :
1436-      IsValue v →
1437-      IsValue <{inl ~τ₁ ~v}>
1438-  | sumInr  (v : Tm) (τ₁ : Ty) :
1439-      IsValue v →
1440-      IsValue <{inr ~τ₁ ~v}>
1441-  -- A list is a value iff its head and tail are values:
1442-  | listNil (τ₁ : Ty) : IsValue <{nil ~τ₁}>
1443-  | listCons (v₁ v₂ : Tm) :
1444-      IsValue v₁ →
1445-      IsValue v₂ →
1446-      IsValue <{~v₁ :: ~v₂}>
1447-  -- A unit is always a value
1448-  | unit : IsValue .unit
1449-  -- A pair is a value if both components are:
1450-  | pair (v₁ v₂ : Tm) :
1451-      IsValue v₁ →
1452-      IsValue v₂ →
1453-      IsValue <{(~v₁, ~v₂)}>

1711-/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1712-context prints as `x ↦ Nat ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1713-partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1714-  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1715-  | `($x:str →ₚ $τ) => do
1716-      unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $τ ; ∅))
1717-  | `($x:str →ₚ $τ ; $G) => do
1718-      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1719-      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1720-        if Stlc.isPlainName x.getString then
1721-          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1722-        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1723-      match τ with
1724-      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1725-      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($τ) ; $G')
1726-  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1727-
1728-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1729-@[app_unexpander HasType]
1730-def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1731-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $τ:stlcTy }>) =>
1732-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $τ }>)
1733-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $τ) =>
1734-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($τ) }>)
1735-  | `($_ $G $t <{ $τ:stlcTy }>) =>
1736-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $τ }>)
1737-  | `($_ $G $t $τ) =>
1738-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($τ) }>)
1739-  | _ => throw ()

7373 --  - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions
7474 --    about the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the
7575 --    addition operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other
8080 --    formal definition, e.g., for implementing a compiler. The Lean

8585 --    informality makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like
8686 --    discussions at the blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more
8787 --    important than nailing down every detail precisely.

9292 --    informal understanding is all that's important.

666658 --  At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use
667659 --  by default?
668---
660+
669661 --  Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
670662 --  definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable,
671663 --  relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand,
674666 --  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
675667 --  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
676668 --  simplify them during proofs.
677---
669+
678670 --  In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both*
679671 --  styles plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to
680672 --  switch between points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
681673 --  `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.

350343 --  It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract

1512---  ### Automation with `solve_by_elim`
1513-
1514---  When experimenting with definitions of programming languages in Lean,
1515---  we often want to see what a particular term steps to - i.e., we want to
1516---  find proofs for goals of the form `t ⟶* t'`. Consider, for example,
1517---  reducing an arithmetic expression using the small-step relation
1518---  `AStep`.
1519-
1520-example : (.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))) ⟶* (.c 10) := by
1521-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c 3) (.c 7))
1522-  · apply Step.plusRight
1523-    · apply IsValue.const
1524-    · apply Step.plus
1525-  · apply Multi.step (y := .c 10)
1526-    · apply Step.plus
1527-    · apply Multi.refl
1528-
1529---  Proofs that one term normalizes to another must repeatedly apply
1530---  `Multi.step` until the term reaches a normal form, with some very
1531---  simple intermediate steps along the way. Thankfully, we can automate
1532---  this process with a new tactic: `solve_by_elim`. When supplied with a
1533---  list of constructors, `solve_by_elim [c₁, c₂, c₃, ...]` will attempt to
1534---  apply these constructors repeatedly to a goal. It will also
1535---  automatically attempt to use simple tactics like `rfl`, `trivial`,
1536---  `congr` and hypotheses from the context in order to solve simple goals.
1537---  So, for example, the proof above also be written:
1538-
1539-example : (.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))) ⟶* (.c 10) := by
1540-  repeat apply Multi.step <;>
1541-    try solve_by_elim [Step.plusRight, Step.plusLeft, Step.plus, IsValue.const]
1542-
1543---  This one script would suffice to prove most concrete reduction
1544---  sequences for this simple language. To make it work for others, we
1545---  would need to supply constructors for those other languages to
1546---  `solve_by_elim`. The languages we will study in this book can grow to a
1547---  large number of constructors for their `Step` relations, so we'd like a
1548---  way to supply all of them to `solve_by_elim` more easily. Luckily, Lean
1549---  supports this. We can register a constructor (or lemma) for use with
1550---  `solve_by_elim` with an `attribute` command:
1551-
1552---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Attributes)
1553---  The command below tags all of these constructors with the `SimpleArith`
1554---  attribute, which we can then use to automatically pull all of these
1555---  constructors in when we use `solve_by_elim`. However, due to a
1556---  limitation of Lean, this attribute needs to be pre-declared in a
1557---  different file; we can't create it here and then immediately use it.
1558---
1559---  For this book, we've predeclared all the attributes we'll use in a file
1560---  called `AttributeDecls.lean`, following the typical pattern from
1561---  libraries like Mathlib.
1562---  END DETAILS
1563-
1564-attribute [SimpleArith] Step.plusRight Step.plusLeft Step.plus IsValue.const
1565-
1566---  This `using` option then tells `solve_by_elim` to try to use every
1567---  constructor we've registered with the supplied attribute:
1568-
1569-example : (.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))) ⟶* (.c 10) := by
1570-  repeat apply Multi.step <;>
1571-    try solve_by_elim using SimpleArith
1572-
1573---  We can package all this up into a dedicated tactic for solving
1574---  reduction sequences, which we'll call `normalize`:
1575-
1576-syntax "normalize" " using " ident,+ : tactic
1577-
1578-macro_rules
1579-  | `(tactic| normalize using $xs,*) =>
1580-    `(tactic|
1581-      first
1582-      | apply Multi.refl
1583-      | (apply Multi.step
1584-         · solve_by_elim (maxDepth := 15) (constructor := false) only using $xs,*
1585-         · normalize using $xs,*))
1586-
1587---  And voilà:
1588-
1589-example : (.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))) ⟶* (.c 10) := by
1590-  normalize using SimpleArith
1591-

1595---  supply the term `e'` yourself.
1596-

1598-  exists (.c 6); constructor
1599-  · normalize using SimpleArith
1600-  · constructor

203197 --  ## Syntax
204198 
230224 --  The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both
231225 --  written inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside
232226 --  the brackets escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
233---
227+
234228 --  - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
235---
229+
236230 --  - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the
237231 --    brackets is the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>`
238232 --    is the variable `x`;
239---
233+
240234 --  - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
241---
235+
242236 --  Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so
243237 --  the same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to
244238 --  typing — for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed
249243 --  associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A bare identifier
250244 --  other than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any
251245 --  Lean expression of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
252---
246+
253247 --  To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line to the
254248 --  category and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is all it takes to add
255249 --  a new type construct.
284278 --  abstraction, the two boolean constants, and conditionals. A binding
285279 --  occurrence — the `x` in `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own,
286280 --  `stlcVar`, and `varStr` turns it into the string that `Tm.abs` stores.
287---
281+
288282 --  Because types and terms share the brackets, each `macro_rules` group
289283 --  says which bracket it belongs to (`kind := tyBracket`,
290284 --  `kind := tmBracket`), and each antiquote in a nested quotation says
292286 --  overlapping case: `Bool` in term position would otherwise quietly
293287 --  become a variable named `Bool`, so that rule rejects it, which also
294288 --  settles which grammar a lone `<{ Bool }>` belongs to.

296290 --  The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for substitution; we

298292 --  than application, so `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁`

507501 --  To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
508---
502+
509503 --  First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear:
510504 --  `true` and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a
511505 --  value.
512---
506+
513507 --  Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
514508 --  invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
515---
509+
516510 --  Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
517---
511+
518512 --  - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e.,
519513 --    only if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be
520514 --    without knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
521---
515+
522516 --  - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t`
523517 --    is one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
524518 --    abstractions.
525---
519+
526520 --  Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the first choice
527521 --  — for example,

536530 --  languages make the second choice — reduction of a function's body only
537531 --  begins when the function is actually applied to an argument.

567559 --  Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.

569561 --  Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
570562 --  variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a
571563 --  STLC term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is,
572564 --  that contains no free variables.

575567 --  *open term*.)

11361098 --  Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
11371099 --  relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit
11381100 --  to make the definitions work.
1139---
1101+
11401102 --  Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively,
11411103 --  we need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed
11421104 --  the binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be
11451107 --  of `x`. Similarly, `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and
11461108 --  typechecking their bodies could require looking up the declared types
11471109 --  of yet more free variables.
1148---
1110+
11491111 --  To keep track of all this, we add a third element to the relation, a
11501112 --  *typing context* `Γ`, which records the types of the variables that may
11511113 --  occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to
11521114 --  types.
1153---
1115+
11541116 --  The new *typing judgment* is written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and informally read as
11551117 --  "term `t` has type `T`, given the types of free variables in `t` as
11561118 --  specified by `Γ`".
1157---
1119+
11581120 --  We'll also write `x ↦ T ; Γ` for "update the partial map `Γ` so that it
11591121 --  maps `x` to `T`," following the notation from the `Typeclasses`
11601122 --  chapter.
1161---
1123+

11631125 --  specifications of the typing relation.

1350---  It's worth noting that `apply_rules` relies on an important property of
1351---  our typing rules - namely, that they are *syntax directed*. A syntax
1352---  directed judgment is one where the syntax of a term completely
1353---  determines which rule can be applied at any given time; only one rule
